content_list.content_text: The Western has been one of Hollywood's staple products since the dawn of cinema. It is undoubtedly the most American of genres, but not always the most acclaimed. Perhaps because they could be produced quickly and on low budgets - the landscape was ready-made and real cowboys were willing to work as extras - Westerns were often dismissed as "pastime" entertainment.

content_list.content_text: In the silent era, pioneers such as Allan Dwan (1885-1981) and Raoul Walsh (1887-1980) often turned out one film a week, from screenplay to final cut. In 1909, the Bison studio arrived in California; in 1910, Broncho Billy Anderson became the first Western star. According to film historian Ed Buscombe's calculations, 213 of the 1,001 American films made that year were Westerns. With the arrival of sound, the genre's popularity declined somewhat, although Western production fell only slightly until the 1960s. Hollywood made more than 800 films in the genre in the 1950s.

Stagecoach (1939), by John Ford (1894-1973), marks the beginning of a period in which Westerns were directed by major filmmakers, such as Ford himself (returning to the genre after more than 10 years away), Michael Curtiz (1886-1962), Fritz Lang (1890-1976) and Howard Hawks (1896-1977), who created famous classics such as Red River (1948) and Rio Bravo (1959).

quote.quote: The Searchers is a film you watch once, twice, and you find more meaning in it, you connect with it on other levels... It's so rich! It's so sumptuous!
quote.author: Martin Scorsese on The Searchers (1956)

content_list.content_text: After World War II, Hollywood's growing interest focused at first on directors such as Ford, and later on the genre itself; the Western came to be seen as part of American mythology, an imaginary battleground between outlaws and the defenders of order, between savagery and civilization.

information.contentText: The set town at Old Tucson was built on a 7:8 scale, which made the characters stand out.

content_list.content_text: The Western is Hollywood's most easily recognizable genre. The James gang in The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford (2007) and the bandits in The Great Train Robbery (1903) wear different hats, but their looks and attitudes clearly identify them as belonging to the same genre.

Westerns are almost always associated with a specific place and historical period: west of the Mississippi River, south of the 49th parallel, north of the Rio Grande, and sometime between 1865 (the end of the American Civil War) and 1890 (when the census declared that the Frontier no longer existed).

All of this is a simplification. There are contemporary Westerns (Lonely Are the Brave (1962)), Canadian Westerns (The Far Country (1954)), Mexican Westerns (Vera Cruz (1954)) and East Coast Westerns (Drums Along the Mohawk (1939)).

information.contentText: Since its release, it has come to be regarded as a masterpiece and one of the greatest and most influential films ever made. It was named the greatest American Western by the American Film Institute in 2008, and placed 12th on the organization's 2007 list of the 100 greatest American films of all time.

content_list.content_text: For some, the Western is a narrative that can be set in Texas, in Vietnam or in outer space: Outland (1981) transposes High Noon (1952) to one of Jupiter's moons. Even so, the set of historical events, characters and places remains at its core.

The Western both celebrates and rewrites the history of the United States. John Ford, the best-known director of Westerns, said that his portrayal of the gunfight at the O.K. Corral in Tombstone, Arizona, in My Darling Clementine (1946), was drawn directly from the account given by Wyatt Earp himself. That story - like the stories of many other Westerns that claim to be based on true events - is debatable; it is said that Westerns are not so much about the West as about other Westerns.

content_list.title: John Ford and Racism
content_list.description: Ford became sympathetic to Native Americans and African Americans late in his career, but he always had to defend himself against accusations of racism. Ethan is not the only racist in The Searchers (1956). Laurie, desperate for Martin to give up his search for Debbie, is equally virulent: "Fetch what home? The leavings of Comanche bucks, sold time and again to the highest bidder, with savage brats of her own?" Being part Cherokee, Martin is apparently more tolerant of interracial mixing. But when his Native American wife (Beulah Archuletta) lies down beside him, he pushes her away. The sadness Martin expresses when she is found dead by the cavalry does not soften the cruelty that the character - and Ford - inflicts on her.

content_list.content_text: Given the weight the myth of the Last Frontier carries in the American psyche, this kind of revisionism is to be expected. Sometimes the process itself becomes the subject of Westerns, whether in iconoclastic films such as Black Patch (1957), by Allen H. Miner (1917-2004), or Ford's own The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance (1962), famous for the line "This is the West, sir. When the legend becomes fact, print the legend".

information.contentTitle: Scene from The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance (1962)
information.contentText: At the end of his account to journalist Maxwell Scott, Stoddard revealed who had really killed Valance, and asked: "You're not going to use the story, Mr. Scott?" The answer was the famous line: "This is the West, sir. When the legend becomes fact, print the legend".

content_list.content_text: Like Altman, Ford knew that the Western was a manufactured legend, but unlike him, Ford saw this in positive terms: only in The Searchers (1956) did he properly explore the dark side of the Western hero. In the late 1930s and early 1940s, the dominant tone of Westerns was one of affirmation mixed with a certain nostalgia.

quote.quote: Shane is so excellent... If I were to make a list of the best American films, it would be on it.
quote.author: Woody Allen on Shane

content_list.content_text: Jesse James (1939) - and its sequel, Fritz Lang's The Return of Frank James (1940) - portrays the famous outlaw brothers as defenders of rural values against the encroachment of Northern banks. In They Died with Their Boots On (1941), Raoul Walsh creates a romanticized image of General Custer, and Buffalo Bill (1944), by William Wellman (1896-1975), does the same.

Ford's My Darling Clementine shows Wyatt Earp (Henry Fonda) arriving in Tombstone and leaving behind a town where cattle rustlers and drunken Indians have been replaced by a church and a school. Shane (1953) offers a more self-critical version of the arrival of the gunfighter with a dark past who rids the town of villainy before returning to the wilderness.

information.contentText: Sergio Leone, in For a Few Dollars More, paid homage to the sequence in which the boy sees Shane shooting.

content_list.content_text: Less affirmative Westerns marked the 1940s and especially the 1950s. Written by screenwriter Carl Foreman, who would soon be added to the FBI's blacklist. Other blacklisted writers who worked on Westerns include Albert Maltz and Ben Maddow, who wrote Broken Arrow (1950) and Johnny Guitar (1954), respectively. Broken Arrow is an early example of a more sympathetic portrayal of Native Americans, as also seen in Apache (1954).

Johnny Guitar (one of the French New Wave directors' favorite films) stars Sterling Hayden and Joan Crawford. Hayden named names before the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1951; a character in the film is forced to do the same.

The "psychological Western" became another hallmark of the postwar period. Pursued (1947), by Raoul Walsh, features a Robert Mitchum haunted by his past in a dark, noir-style landscape. Paul Newman is an unbalanced Billy the Kid in The Left Handed Gun (1958), and in The Gunfighter (1950) Gregory Peck plays a man pursued by his own reputation as the "fastest gun", knowing that some ambitious young man will turn up to take his place.

information.contentText: As suggested by the striking image on the Johnny Guitar posters, the film's story revolves around strong female characters.

content_list.content_text: The Hollywood Western survived into the 1960s and beyond, driven by a new generation of directors who moved from television into the film industry, among them Robert Altman, Arthur Penn (1922-2010) and Sam Peckinpah (1925-1984). Peckinpah was particularly important for passionately revisiting some Western traditions, as in Ride the High Country (1962), and more violently in The Wild Bunch (1969) and Pat Garrett & Billy the Kid (1973).

The genre even survived the box office failure of Heaven's Gate (1980). Hollywood took a break, but went on producing teen Westerns, Westerns with gay themes and, in 2007, a remake of 3:10 to Yuma (1957), the kind of efficient combination of outlaw characters and landscape that became characteristic of 1950s films.

movies.title: The Searchers
movies.overview: As a Civil War veteran spends years searching for a young niece captured by Indians, his motivation becomes increasingly questionable.

movies.title: High Noon
movies.overview: Will Kane, the sheriff of a small town in New Mexico, learns a notorious outlaw he put in jail has been freed, and will be arriving on the noon train. Knowing the outlaw and his gang are coming to kill him, Kane is determined to stand his ground, so he gathers a posse from among the local townspeople.

movies.title: Red River
movies.overview: Headstrong Thomas Dunson starts a thriving Texas cattle ranch with the help of his faithful trail hand, Groot, and his protégé, Matthew Garth, an orphan Dunson took under his wing when Matt was a boy. In need of money following the Civil War, Dunson and Matt lead a cattle drive to Missouri, where they will get a better price than locally, but the crotchety older man and his willful young partner begin to butt heads on the exhausting journey.

movies.title: Lonely Are the Brave
movies.overview: A fiercely independent cowboy arranges to have himself locked up in jail in order to then escape with an old friend who has been sentenced to the penitentiary.

movies.title: The Left Handed Gun
movies.overview: When a crooked sheriff murder his employer, William "Billy the Kid" Bonney decides to avenge the death by killing the man responsible, throwing the lives of everyone around him into turmoil, and endangering the General Amnesty set up by Governor Wallace to bring peace to the New Mexico Territory.

movies.title: Rio Bravo
movies.overview: The sheriff of a small town in southwest Texas must keep custody of a murderer whose brother, a powerful rancher, is trying to help him escape. After a friend is killed trying to muster support for him, he and his deputies - a disgraced drunk and a cantankerous old cripple - must find a way to hold out against the rancher's hired guns until the marshal arrives. In the meantime, matters are complicated by the presence of a young gunslinger - and a mysterious beauty who just came in on the last stagecoach.

movies.title: Johnny Guitar
movies.overview: On the outskirts of town, the hard-nosed Vienna owns a saloon frequented by the undesirables of the region, including Dancin' Kid and his gang. Another patron of Vienna's establishment is Johnny Guitar, a former gunslinger and her lover. When a heist is pulled in town that results in a man's death, Emma Small, Vienna's rival, rallies the townsfolk to take revenge on Vienna's saloon – even without proof of her wrongdoing.

The Western holds on to its reign as one of the most popular genres, and one of the most important movements in cinema takes place in France: the French New Wave.
